strengths: VS-BENCH targets an important and underexplored intersection of computer vision, multimodal agents, and multi-agent interaction. Its eight environments cover cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings rather than reducing evaluation to a single game type.
The combination of offline next-action prediction and online interaction is useful in principle, and evaluating 14 commercial and open-source VLMs provides a broad empirical snapshot.

The paper reports per-environment results, raw and normalized returns, variability for online evaluations, text-only comparisons, prompting analyses, behavioral summaries, and qualitative failures. These analyses expose concrete limitations such as poor state tracking, information-asymmetry errors, and weak visual dynamics understanding.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with detailed appendices describing environments, dataset construction, model versions, and evaluation opponents.

The main empirical conclusion—that current VLMs remain weak interactive game agents—is supported qualitatively by the low raw returns and numerous failures, even if the exact aggregate rankings are less reliable.
weaknesses: The central offline metric has a serious construct-validity problem. A next action in these partially observed games is generally policy-dependent, stochastic, and often non-unique; predicting one logged action is therefore not equivalent to inferring beliefs or demonstrating theory of mind. The claimed 100% oracle merely has access to the recorded label and is not a meaningful strategic upper bound.

Offline data generation can bias model comparisons. Hanabi labels are predominantly generated by two Doubao models, while Pong labels come from trajectories of o4-mini and Doubao, which are themselves evaluated on the benchmark. Other games use narrow hand-coded strategy mixtures. Consequently, accuracy may reward imitation or recognition of the selected source policies rather than general strategic reasoning.

The normalized-return aggregation lacks a consistent interpretation because several stated 'optimal' references are not optimal. Breakthrough uses depth-5 heuristic minimax, Hanabi uses a reported MAPPO policy, Overcooked assumes two deliveries, and mixed-motive games use particular welfare-oriented heuristics. In Kuhn Poker, both the Nash reference and many models have nearly identical rounded raw returns, making normalization unstable. Averaging these heterogeneous normalized quantities into one overall score can therefore yield misleading rankings.

Online estimates are too noisy to support fine-grained model rankings: most environments use only 10 episodes, Breakthrough uses 20 binary games, temperature is 1.0, and many reported standard deviations are comparable to or larger than the means. No confidence intervals, paired tests, or significance analysis are provided. For example, multiple claimed differences in Tables 2 and 6 are small relative to their variability.

Self-play between two instances of the same model conflates individual decision quality, convention compatibility, and correlated failure modes. Competitive evaluation likewise uses only one fixed opponent per game. Thus the results provide limited evidence for the claimed robustness under non-stationary multi-agent dynamics or adaptation to other agents.

The multimodal conclusion is overstated. Only three environments are examined, results are mixed at the individual-model level, and no statistical testing is reported. Text descriptions can also expose clean symbolic state information and remove the perception burden, so poorer image-based performance does not establish that multimodal observations are intrinsically unhelpful or that the two inputs contain equivalent information.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: exact prompts, action-parsing rules, invalid-output handling, API retry behavior, and implementation details needed to reproduce interactive trajectories are not provided. The code/data locations are blank in the reviewed PDF. These omissions are especially consequential for API models and long sequential evaluations.

Some interpretations exceed the evidence. The agents do not learn concurrently, so the repeated characterization of the evaluated dynamics as non-stationary through concurrent learning is inaccurate. Behavioral counts from only 10 self-play episodes are also insufficient to substantiate broad claims about models being prosocial or self-interested.

strengths: The benchmark targets an important and underexplored intersection of computer vision, multimodal agents, and multi-agent strategic interaction. Its eight environments span cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings and include board, card, grid-world, and pixel-based games.

The empirical coverage is substantial: fourteen commercial and open-source VLMs are evaluated using both offline next-action prediction and online interaction. Reporting per-environment results, raw returns, variances, and model versions is useful.

The comparison between visual and text state representations is informative evidence of a perception bottleneck, even though the paper overstates the strength of the conclusion. The qualitative failure cases also illustrate concrete errors involving partial observability, state tracking, and defensive planning.

The manuscript is generally well organized, visually clear, and candid about limitations such as the lack of human baselines, the predominance of two-player games, and evaluation against a limited set of partners.
weaknesses: The offline metric does not cleanly measure strategic reasoning or theory of mind. It measures agreement with one sampled next action from a particular policy. Several data-generating policies are explicitly stochastic, including mixed Nash strategies in Kuhn Poker, so the sampled action can be intrinsically unpredictable from the observation. Nevertheless, the paper uses a 100% label-replay 'oracle' and interprets the gap to 100% as a reasoning deficiency. No Bayes ceiling, annotator agreement, policy-distribution scoring, or likelihood-based metric is provided.

The offline datasets often test imitation of narrow generators rather than general opponent modeling. Hanabi labels largely come from two Doubao models, Pong labels come from the two best evaluated VLMs, and the three mixed-motive datasets use small, manually specified heuristic families. A model can therefore score by recognizing these generators or shortest-path behavior, while a strategically sound alternative action is marked wrong. There is no held-out-policy or cross-partner evaluation.

The normalized online score is not technically well founded as a common 0–100 measure. Several references called 'optimal' are merely heuristics: Breakthrough uses depth-5 minimax with a hand-designed evaluation because it beats a modest MCTS opponent, while the mixed-motive references use fixed movement rules. In Kuhn Poker, Table 4 reports an optimal raw return of 0.0 and a random return of -0.1; normalizing by this very small denominator amplifies tiny, rounded differences into values such as 92.9. Averaging these heterogeneous and sometimes unstable normalized scores across games makes the headline 24.3% difficult to interpret.

Most online evaluations use only ten episodes, despite substantial stochasticity and very large standard deviations. For example, several normalized results have standard deviations comparable to or exceeding their means. The paper nevertheless ranks models and repeatedly uses terms such as 'significant' without confidence intervals, statistical tests, or repeated-seed analyses. The CoT and multimodal comparisons are especially underpowered and contain numerous model/environment cases that contradict the broad aggregate claims.

Self-play between two instances of the same model confounds individual decision quality with same-model coordination and social preference. Conversely, each competitive game uses only one conventional opponent. These protocols do not support the stronger claims about adaptability, robustness to non-stationary agents, or general strategic competence; the evaluated VLM policies do not learn or adapt during play.

Reproducibility is insufficient in the submitted manuscript. It does not provide the actual prompts, parsing and retry rules, treatment of invalid actions, normalization equations, random seeds, inference settings beyond temperature/token limits, or enough implementation detail to reconstruct the visual-to-action interface. The displayed code/data links are empty, and the open-source model entries say only 'huggingface link.' These omissions are particularly consequential because prompt format and invalid-action handling can strongly affect interactive-agent results.

Some analyses are descriptive rather than rigorous. Social behavior conclusions are drawn from only ten same-model self-play episodes, the visual-versus-text comparison may advantage text by supplying a clean symbolic state representation, and a few selected qualitative failures cannot establish that the stated failure modes are prevalent. Overall, the benchmark premise and experimental effort are worthwhile, but the validity of the principal metrics and headline comparisons currently favors rejection.

strengths: VS-BENCH addresses a timely and underexplored problem: evaluating multimodal agents in genuinely multi-agent settings rather than single-agent or text-only tasks. Its eight environments span cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive interactions and include card, board, grid-world, and pixel-based games.

The combination of offline next-action prediction and online episodic interaction is valuable. These views expose different limitations: models can sometimes anticipate actions yet still fail to optimize long-horizon returns.

The empirical scope is strong: fourteen commercial and open-source VLMs are evaluated, with exact commercial model versions reported. Per-environment results, raw returns, standard deviations for online evaluation, and random/reference policies make the principal trends reasonably transparent.

The paper provides useful analyses beyond a leaderboard, including multimodal-versus-text observations, chain-of-thought prompting, social behavior, and concrete failure cases involving private information, visual-state recognition, rule application, defense, and temporal control.

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear. Environment rules, dataset construction procedures, and most evaluation protocols receive substantial appendix documentation. The supported finding that present VLMs remain weak interactive game agents is potentially useful to both vision-language and agent research.
weaknesses: The offline metric does not cleanly establish the claimed theory-of-mind or strategic-reasoning ability. Exact next-action prediction conflates visual perception, policy imitation, and strategic inference. Several targets come from fixed heuristics, minimax agents, or particular VLMs; Kuhn Poker explicitly uses stochastic mixed strategies, for which a realized action cannot generally be predicted with 100% accuracy. Labeling the observed action as an oracle score of 100 therefore gives a misleading performance ceiling.

The normalized online score depends on reference policies repeatedly called optimal even when optimality is not established. The Breakthrough reference is a depth-5 heuristic minimax policy that the authors acknowledge is not guaranteed optimal; several mixed-motive references are hand-designed heuristics; and Overcooked optimality is asserted from completing two deliveries. Consequently, the headline 24.3% gap to 'optimal' should be interpreted as performance relative to selected references, not a calibrated fraction of optimal ability.

Online estimates are frequently based on only ten self-play episodes, despite very large reported variability—for example, several Hanabi, Breakthrough, and Poker standard deviations are comparable to their means. The paper gives no confidence intervals or significance tests for model rankings or aggregate findings, and the overall score averages heterogeneous normalized quantities without uncertainty. Some comparative conclusions are therefore less stable than their presentation suggests.

Self-play between two instances of the same model measures a mixture of individual competence and same-model compatibility. Competitive evaluation likewise uses only one conventional opponent per game. Without cross-play or a population of opponents, the benchmark provides limited evidence about robustness, adaptation, or general multi-agent competence; the manuscript appropriately notes this limitation, but it materially narrows the claims.

The multimodal contribution is meaningful but somewhat overstated. Most visual observations are clean renderings of symbolic game states, and corresponding text descriptions can often encode those states losslessly. The three-game modality comparison also produces mixed per-model outcomes, so the broad conclusion that multimodal observations are generally detrimental is stronger than the reported evidence warrants.

Reproducibility from the manuscript alone remains incomplete: exact prompts, action-parsing and invalid-output handling, random seeds, the explicit normalization equation, and some reference-policy implementation details are not reported. These omissions are especially important because API models use temperature 1.0 and online results have high variance. This is a substantive documentation concern, although a complete promised code/data release could mitigate it.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and underexplored problem: evaluating general-purpose VLMs in visually grounded multi-agent interactions rather than single-agent or text-only settings. The ten environments span cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive games and include partial observability, spatial control, and social dilemmas.

The evaluation is unusually broad in model coverage, testing fifteen commercial and open-source VLMs with identifiable model versions. Reporting perception, next-action prediction, and interactive returns provides more diagnostic value than a single aggregate benchmark score.

The appendices provide environment rules, dataset-generation procedures, raw decision-making results, and model-level standard deviations. The text-only comparisons, CoT experiments, persona interventions, qualitative failures, human baseline, and preliminary three-player experiments are useful supplementary analyses.

The main empirical conclusion—that current VLMs perform much better on static state extraction than on sustained interactive control—is supported consistently across many environments and model families. The benchmark and environments could therefore become useful research infrastructure if the evaluation protocol is strengthened.
weaknesses: The strategic-reasoning metric has a serious construct-validity problem. Its labels are actions produced by heterogeneous sources, including particular VLMs, human trajectories, minimax/Nash agents, and hand-coded heuristics. Predicting those policy-specific actions is not necessarily equivalent to inferring beliefs or intentions, especially when the evaluated model is not given the demonstrator's identity or policy. Rebalancing action classes and manually mixing strategies further separates the reported accuracy from prediction under natural gameplay. Thus the strong interpretation as a theory-of-mind evaluation is not adequately established.

The perception results can substantially overstate competence. Several tasks use unweighted per-cell accuracy on sparse grids, where empty cells dominate; for example, a structured majority baseline could score highly in the 5x5 social-dilemma grids. Nevertheless, the only reported baseline is an artificial 0% "Random" score. The conclusion that all models have adequate perception, based on 67.8–84.9% aggregate accuracy, is therefore unsupported without meaningful majority, format-aware, or object-level baselines.

Decision-making estimates are statistically weak for the claims and rankings presented. Most environments use only ten episodes per model, while the raw results show very large variability—for example, normalized Breakthrough and Hanabi results often have standard deviations of tens of points. Table 4 and the overall ranking omit uncertainty, and there are no confidence intervals, repeated-seed analysis, or significance tests. Consequently, many model comparisons and analysis claims such as significant CoT or persona effects are not demonstrated reliably.

The normalized return is not consistently anchored to a genuine optimum. The paper acknowledges that the Breakthrough depth-5 minimax policy is not guaranteed optimal; MPE uses a heuristic value of zero; mixed-motive games use selected heuristic policies; and Pong combines normalized score and survival rewards with manually chosen weights. Averaging these heterogeneous 0–100 quantities gives an accessible summary but does not justify repeated claims about a calibrated "gap to optimal performance."

The interactive protocol is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. The manuscript does not provide the complete base prompts, conversation-state and history policy, action parsing rules, treatment of malformed or invalid outputs, retry behavior, API seed handling, or full per-environment rollout settings. These choices can materially affect agent performance. Self-play against an identical model or evaluation against one fixed conventional opponent also conflates strategic ability with partner/opponent compatibility and does not support claims about adaptability or generalization.

The human comparison lacks necessary methodological detail, including participant allocation across games, training or practice, per-game sample sizes, randomization, and uncertainty. Reporting that a model surpasses a particular percentage of the 26 participants is therefore difficult to interpret as a robust human-level comparison.

There are consequential consistency and presentation errors. Most notably, Table 9 is described as covering Coin Dilemma, Monster Hunt, and Battle of the Colors, but its columns are labeled Hanabi, Breakthrough, and Monster Hunt. Other model naming and best-chat-model descriptions are inconsistent. These are correctable, but they impede verification of the persona analysis. Overall, the benchmark is promising, but the metric validity, normalization, and statistical support are material weaknesses that currently outweigh its contribution.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and comparatively underexplored intersection: evaluating general-purpose VLM agents in visually grounded multi-agent settings rather than only static or single-agent tasks.
VS-Bench has substantial breadth, covering ten cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive environments and fifteen commercial and open-source VLMs.

Separating perception, next-action prediction, and interactive decision-making is potentially useful diagnostically. The appendix also reports raw returns, model versions, environment rules, and several implementation details.
The text-only, chain-of-thought, persona, human-baseline, failure-case, and preliminary three-player studies provide useful perspectives beyond a single aggregate leaderboard.
The reported results consistently expose large limitations of current VLM agents, which could motivate work on multimodal coordination and opponent modeling.
weaknesses: The central strategic-reasoning metric has weak construct validity. Its 'ground-truth' actions are frequently produced by selected VLMs or hand-designed heuristics: for example, KAZ, Pong, and MPE use actions from strong reasoning models, Hanabi uses Doubao model trajectories, and the mixed-motive games use fixed heuristic personas. A strategically reasonable alternative action is normally counted as wrong. Consequently, accuracy measures imitation of particular policies more directly than theory of mind or strategic reasoning, and it may favor models related to the label generators.

The claimed oracle-normalized decision scores are not anchored to genuine optimal policies consistently. The paper calls a depth-5 heuristic minimax agent optimal for Breakthrough while acknowledging it is not guaranteed optimal; MPE uses a heuristic value of zero; the mixed-motive games use handcrafted policies; and other environments use heterogeneous RL or rule-based references. Setting all these references to 100 and averaging across games produces an overall score whose cardinal meaning is unclear. Likewise, the 100% 'oracle' for next-action prediction is tautological rather than a substantive strategic baseline.

Most interactive evaluations use only ten episodes, despite very large observed variance. Table 6 reports standard deviations comparable to or larger than means for several games, while the main rankings omit uncertainty and the paper provides no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or sensitivity analysis. Claims such as significant CoT improvement and precise model ordering are therefore insufficiently supported.

Self-play with the same model is used for most cooperative and mixed-motive evaluations, while several competitive environments use one fixed conventional opponent. Performance consequently conflates an agent's individual capability with compatibility with its own policy or one specific opponent. The paper does not evaluate robustness against a diverse opponent or partner population, limiting claims about adaptation, general strategic ability, and non-stationary multi-agent interaction.

The perception evaluation can substantially overstate useful visual understanding. Grid-cell accuracy equally rewards empty and occupied cells, so environments such as the 8x8 Breakthrough board can yield high scores by recognizing abundant empty space. The paper reports an artificial random baseline of zero rather than meaningful majority, random-guess, or object-conditioned baselines and does not break out accuracy on strategically important entities. Thus, the conclusion that all models have 'adequate perception' for downstream reasoning is not established.

Several analyses overreach their evidence. The text-only descriptions appear to provide structured state information rather than a controlled modality substitution, the CoT study covers only three games without significance testing, and the human study gives insufficient details about participant assignment, training, game expertise, per-environment sample sizes, and uncertainty. These results are informative pilots but do not justify broad conclusions.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate. The manuscript's dataset and code links are blank, open-model entries say only 'huggingface link,' the complete base prompts and parsing procedures are not included, and important details such as seeds and failure/retry handling for proprietary APIs are missing.

There are also presentation inconsistencies, although these are secondary to the methodological issues: Table 9 describes persona results for the three mixed-motive games but labels its columns Hanabi, Breakthrough, and Monster Hunt; o4-mini appears in raw results and dataset construction without being part of the stated fifteen-model main evaluation; and some plots are too small for comfortable inspection.

strengths: VS-BENCH addresses a timely and underexplored problem: evaluating vision-language models in genuinely interactive multi-agent settings rather than single-agent or text-only tasks. Its ten environments span cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive interactions and cover varied strategic properties such as partial observability, simultaneous actions, spatial reasoning, and long-term coordination.

The three-part evaluation—perception, next-action prediction, and interactive decision-making—is diagnostically useful. In particular, the results distinguish relatively strong visual state extraction (best overall perception accuracy 84.9%) from much weaker strategic reasoning (46.6% best accuracy) and control (31.4 best normalized return).

The empirical scope is substantial: fifteen commercial and open-source VLMs are evaluated per environment, with 400 examples per game for each offline evaluation dimension. The paper also reports raw decision-making returns and standard deviations, exact commercial-model versions, environment-specific protocols, random and reference-policy baselines, and preliminary three-player results.

The supplementary analyses add value beyond a leaderboard. Text-only comparisons help isolate the cost of visual grounding; IO/CoT comparisons provide evidence for test-time reasoning effects; persona experiments expose sensitivity of social behavior to instructions; and the 26-participant study provides a useful, if imperfect, human reference.

The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and unusually detailed for a benchmark submission. Environment construction, sampling strategies, rewards, reference agents, and failure cases are documented, and the promised code/data release should make the benchmark potentially useful to the community.
weaknesses: The strategic-reasoning metric is not a clean measure of theory of mind. In several environments, the target action is generated by another VLM, a hand-coded heuristic, or one particular search policy. Accuracy therefore partly measures imitation of the chosen behavior generator; a strategically valid alternative action can be marked wrong, except in a few grid games where equivalent transitions are explicitly accepted. The paper should frame this as next-action prediction rather than direct evidence of inferred beliefs, desires, or intentions.

The decision-making estimates are often based on only 10 episodes, despite substantial stochasticity. Table 6 shows very large standard deviations—for example, Monster Hunt and several Hanabi results—so some model rankings and claims of meaningful differences are weakly supported. Confidence intervals, repeated-seed comparisons, or significance tests are absent.

The reported “oracle” and “optimal” references are heterogeneous and sometimes explicitly non-optimal: Breakthrough uses depth-limited minimax, MPE uses an assumed heuristic value, and mixed-motive games use selected heuristic conventions. Normalizing every game between a random policy and these different reference policies, then averaging across games, produces an intuitive summary but not a calibrated percentage of globally optimal performance. Calling the top endpoint “oracle” or interpreting 31.4 as a precise gap to optimality overstates the evidence.

Self-play with identical models is informative but conflates individual competence, compatibility with a copy of itself, and equilibrium selection. Evaluation against only one conventional opponent in several competitive games also provides limited evidence about robustness or adaptation. The paper acknowledges the need for a population of opponents, but this remains a material limitation of the current benchmark.

Some perception scores can be inflated by class imbalance. Grid-cell accuracy in sparse boards rewards predicting empty cells, and the Hanabi score gives most weight to card-information units. Per-class, occupied-cell, or object-level metrics would make the claim that all models have “adequate perception” more convincing.

The human baseline lacks enough methodological detail to interpret its aggregate score confidently: per-game participant counts, prior experience, instruction or practice time, grouping procedure, compensation structure, and uncertainty are not reported. Human scores are also compared with model means without statistical analysis.

Reproducibility currently relies heavily on the external release. The manuscript does not provide the general agent prompts, parsing and invalid-action policy, API retry behavior, random seeds, or full human-study protocol. There are also correctable presentation errors, including the mislabeled columns in Table 9 (named Hanabi and Breakthrough despite describing three mixed-motive games) and inconsistent reported GPT-4.1 human-comparison values (4.8 versus 4.4).
